items.title: Ingrid Sertso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

ctx.x: But some of them along the way, as you say, either they repress it or they — over the years I’ve done some work with public school teachers with music programs. And these are not music teachers. And you always get a number of people who say, “Oh when they passed out the rhythm I was hiding under the bed.” You know, they almost are proud that they can’t find the beat.

It’s buried deep, unless they dig it out. There was a beautiful thing at the Creative Music Studio where a student walked out of Dollar Brand’s, Abdullah Ibrahim’s workshop and cried. A guy. And I said, “What’s wrong?” And he said, “I’m not black. I will never be able to be a drummer, a good drummer.” So I said, “No, you go right back in.” And I walked up to Dollar and I told him what the student had said. That’s all I told him. Wow. This is sometimes a hard question. Did you and Karl feel like over the years you were doing something that was an important part of jazz history? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
